newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - CRB/GSCI indices steady so far in 1997.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - CRB/GSCI indices steady so far in 1997.

text.p: Weakness in the energy, precious metals and tropical products sectors have offset gains in the grains and base metal sectors in the first few weeks of the new year, leaving benchmark U.S. commodity indices little changed from year-end 1996, analysts said.

"Apart from soybeans and coffee there are not many bull markets out there right now, and 1997 could shape up in a similar trading range as 1996 for the CRB (Commodities Research Bureau Index)," Merrill Lynch's New York-based director of commodity research, Bill O'Neill said.
"Certainly there's not much sign of commodity-led inflation out there," he said.
The CRB Index was at 240.76 midmorning Wednesday, off its high for 1997 so far at 244.30 on January 16, and little changed from the 239.61 on December 31.
The Goldman Sachs Commodity Index (GSCI), which is more heavily weighted in the energy sector, was at 209.60, down on its December 31 level of 215.26.
But the GSCI did see a new record high at 231.82 on January 6, as crude oil prices rallied in early January to test the five year highs seen in December.

The GSCI Total Returns Index was up only 0.05 percent for the 1997 year-to-date, but the Returns Index is up 41.64 pct for the past 12 months, compared to 29.75 pct for the S&P500 index on a comparable basis.

The GSCI Total Returns Index is based on investing in commodities in the GSCI index as an asset class, by buying the nearby active CME GSCI futures contract, and rolling it forward each month near the contract's expiry.
On this basis, GSCI energy sector returns are up 79.38 pct in the past 12 months, led by a 108.39 pct return in crude oil returns.
Front month NYMEX crude oil prices have remained above their 250-day (yearly) moving average since January 1996.

But "the most recent phase of the current rally in the past seven weeks (in crude oil) has been notable in that momentum readings have thus far failed to confirm the recent push toward $26.00 level," Smith Barney New York technical analyst Rick Lorusso said.
Front month NYMEX March crude oil was trading around $24.41 a barrel midmorning Wednesday.

"The changing supply picture in the Atlantic Basin, alongside powerful seasonal tendencies, has led us to a more bearish medium-to-longer term view on crude, under all but the most extreme US and European winter weather circumstances," Smith Barney's Houston-based energy analyst John Saucer said.

Iraq has quickly lined up a maximum of $1.0 billion in crude oil sales for the first 90-days of its UN oil-for-food deal, with some 21 companies approved to lift just under 500,000 barrels per day during the period.
Total OPEC crude oil supply is seen edging up to 26.5 million bpd in the first quarter 1997, while non-OPEC supply is seen rising to 45.4 million bpd, analysts said.

While low US and European crude oil inventories may limit any near month price weakness, rising supply will temporarily run into low demand in the first quarter also, as seasonal US refinery maintenance is expected to be the most extensive for several years, analysts said.
"But for now we remain overweight in the energy complex and we expect to remain underweight in precious metals for an extended period," O'Neill said.

"The most recent blow to gold was the confirmation by the Dutch central bank it had sold 300 tonnes of gold over the past few months, and we anticipate additional European central bank sales in coming months."
Spot gold bullion prices saw new three year lows around $349.50 an ounce overnight, while the nearby active February COMEX gold futures saw fresh life-of contract lows at $349.80.
